questions.q: What does LEN('Hello   ') (with three trailing spaces) return?
options: 8 — LEN counts every character including trailing spaces
An error, since trailing spaces are invalid
questions.explain: LEN() specifically ignores trailing spaces when counting, which can be surprising.

questions.q: Does LEN() ignore leading spaces the same way it ignores trailing ones?
options: Yes, both leading and trailing spaces are ignored
LEN() ignores all spaces anywhere in the string
No — leading spaces DO count toward the length
LEN() cannot process strings containing spaces at all
questions.explain: Only trailing spaces are excluded from the count — leading spaces are counted normally.

questions.q: Why does the trailing-space behavior of LEN() matter more for CHAR columns than VARCHAR?
options: CHAR pads values with trailing spaces to reach its declared length, and LEN() won't count that padding
There's no actual difference between how LEN() treats CHAR vs. VARCHAR
VARCHAR always has trailing spaces; CHAR never does
LEN() cannot be used on CHAR columns at all
questions.explain: This directly ties back to Lesson 41 — CHAR's padding behavior interacts with LEN()'s trailing-space exclusion.

questions.q: Do UPPER() and LOWER() change the underlying stored data?
options: They modify the data only when combined with GROUP BY
No — like every function used so far, they only affect the query's output
Only UPPER() modifies the data; LOWER() does not
Yes, they permanently modify the table's data
questions.explain: Consistent with every other function in this course — these are output transformations, not data modifications.

questions.q: Why might you use UPPER() on both sides of a WHERE comparison, like WHERE UPPER(LastName) = UPPER('smith')?
options: Because WHERE cannot compare lowercase text otherwise
To guarantee a case-insensitive comparison regardless of the server's default collation settings
It has no practical effect and is purely stylistic
To make the query run faster in all cases
questions.explain: Most SQL Server setups already compare case-insensitively by default, but explicit UPPER()/UPPER() removes any doubt.
